what: Folding two spellings of one join URL into the identity they share — every input and the answer cal_core::normalize_join_url must give.
why:
These answers were MEASURED, not chosen. They are what `shared/meetingLinkGrouping.ts` produced with `new URL()` before the rule crossed into the core, so the table is the record of a behaviour that had to survive the move rather than a fresh opinion about what folding should do.

Four rows are the whole reason a real parser is used instead of a hand-rolled fold: a default port that disappears, dot segments that resolve, and an internationalised host that becomes punycode from either spelling. A fold written by hand would answer that `münchen.example.com` and `xn--mnchen-3ya.example.com` are two hosts, and the failure is silent — a group simply stops being offered.

cases.note: The ordinary case, and the one that must not move.
Scheme and host are case-insensitive; the path and query are not.
A trailing slash inside the QUERY stays. Only the path is stripped — a meeting id and password live in the query, and two links that differ there are two meetings.
Surrounding space, which a copied link carries all the time.
Percent-encoding is left exactly as it stands; re-encoding it would change the identity.
The DEFAULT port disappears. A hand-rolled fold would keep it and read this as a different meeting from the row above.
A bare slash folds to the same thing as no path.
Dot segments RESOLVE. A hand-rolled fold would not.
An internationalised host in its punycode spelling.
The SAME host spelled with the umlaut. One host, one identity — and the reason this crate takes a URL parser rather than folding by hand.
Nothing to parse: compared as it stands rather than inventing a normalisation. Two identical strings still match.
Not a join URL, and never will be. Written down so the odd shape the fold gives it is a recorded fact rather than a surprise.
